overview.text: Vitamin D, also called calciferol, is a fat-soluble vitamin with two main sources: certain foods and supplements, and vitamin D₃ made in the skin after exposure to ultraviolet light. Before the body can use it fully, it is converted first in the liver and then mainly in the kidneys. Its key role is helping the intestine absorb calcium; it also helps maintain phosphate levels needed for normal bone growth and mineralization. Too little vitamin D can weaken bones and cause rickets in children or osteomalacia in adults. The two main forms are D₂ (ergocalciferol) and D₃ (cholecalciferol); some foods, including milk in the United States, are fortified with it.

key_facts.text: Vitamin D is fat-soluble and is also known as calciferol.
Ultraviolet light can trigger vitamin D production in the skin; the amount produced varies with factors such as season and skin pigmentation.
Vitamin D helps the gut absorb calcium, supporting normal bone formation and mineralization.
The two main forms in foods and supplements are D₂ (ergocalciferol) and D₃ (cholecalciferol).
In the United States, most milk is fortified with vitamin D; few foods naturally contain much of it.
